dek_candidates: A B Infrabuild builds railway platforms, bridges and roads around Mumbai and sells ready-mix concrete from a plant in Thane. Its DRHP shows revenue falling from ₹90.21 crore in FY2015 to ₹60.53 crore in FY2018, a ₹11.30 crore working-capital object, and one customer that was 57% of FY2018 revenue.

The filing discloses a promoter holding 90.949% before the issue, 44,28,000 shares on offer at a price left blank, and the money going to working capital and general corporate purposes. Here is what the DRHP says, page by page.

Every figure must be converted to ₹ crore in the prose while keeping the lakh figure visible; a reader should never have to work out whether ₹314.66 lakhs is a lot or a little.

Do not characterise the offer as a fresh issue. The excerpts show proceeds going to the company and name no selling shareholder, which is suggestive, not conclusive. Say what the filing shows and say what it does not.
The valuation section will feel thin. Resist filling it. A reader who is told plainly that the price is blank and the peer column headings are missing knows more than one handed a fabricated table.

Do not reach for the phrase 'order book' as though it were a guarantee: the filing itself says contracts in the order book may be adjusted, cancelled or suspended by clients and that the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenue.
Keep the risks section to five. The filing contains more; depth on the customer-concentration risk is worth more to the reader than a longer list.

beats.beat: Define the two segments in plain words before naming them: a contracting arm that physically builds things for public bodies, and a materials arm that makes and sells ready-mix concrete — the pre-mixed, truck-delivered concrete used on construction sites.

What the contracting arm actually builds, in the filing's own categories: railway platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and track laying; bridge works across beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss types; and bituminous and concrete road construction.

How a job is won — this is the single most important mechanic in the filing. A client floats a tender; there is a pre-bid meeting; contractors bid only if they meet the eligibility conditions; the work is awarded to the lowest quote by letter of acceptance; the winner deposits a performance guarantee; then drawings are issued and the site handed over.
The consequence of a lowest-quote system: the company's revenue depends on its bids being accepted, and a lower winning bid is the price of winning. The filing names this directly as a risk.

Who the customers are: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, MMRDA, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India, plus private names including Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.

How concentrated that customer list is. Top customers were 57% of revenue for the year ended March 31, 2018; Western Railway alone was 52% of orders on hand. The filing uses Indian Railways as the name for the customer that was 57% of FY2018 revenue.

Footprint and assets: work is concentrated in Mumbai and being extended across Maharashtra; the RMC facility at Kashimira, Thane district is described as the company's plant, with the filing's strengths section also pointing to box-pushing techniques and a management team it says has more than 20 years in the industry.

business.heading: What the company does, and how it wins work
business.purpose: Explain the two revenue engines, the tender mechanic that produces the work, who the customers are, and how dependent the whole thing is on a small number of them.

beats.beat: Revenue from operations, in the filing's column order (latest period first): FY2018 ₹6,053.05 lakhs, FY2017 ₹7,344.47 lakhs, FY2016 ₹7,452.76 lakhs, FY2015 ₹9,021.12 lakhs, with a fifth period shown at ₹8,661.35 lakhs. In crore: ₹60.53 crore in FY2018 against ₹90.21 crore in FY2015.
The direction, stated plainly: revenue has fallen across the restated periods, from ₹9,021.12 lakhs in FY2015 to ₹6,053.05 lakhs in FY2018 — the fall the filing itself describes.

Profit after adjustments went the other way: ₹314.66 lakhs (₹3.15 crore) in FY2018 against ₹15.86 lakhs (₹0.16 crore) in FY2017, with ₹32.63 lakhs, ₹78.36 lakhs and ₹95.95 lakhs in the earlier periods shown. The FY2017-to-FY2018 jump is the one the filing flags.

EBITDA as the filing labels it — profit before interest, depreciation and tax — was ₹928.80 lakhs (₹9.29 crore) in FY2018 against ₹676.19 lakhs (₹6.76 crore) in FY2017, ₹783.31 lakhs, ₹945.78 lakhs and ₹784.46 lakhs in the periods shown before that.

Put those two together and say what the reader should notice: revenue fell from ₹73.44 crore to ₹60.53 crore between FY2017 and FY2018, while EBITDA rose from ₹6.76 crore to ₹9.29 crore and profit rose roughly twentyfold. The excerpts carry both trends but no explanation for them.

The balance sheet: total assets were ₹8,232.15 lakhs (₹82.32 crore) in FY2018 against ₹7,536.93 lakhs (₹75.37 crore) in FY2017, ₹6,295.21 lakhs, ₹7,266.50 lakhs and ₹7,062.34 lakhs in the periods shown before that.

Debt, and its shape: short-term borrowings were ₹3,537.35 lakhs (₹35.37 crore) in FY2018 against ₹3,312.08 lakhs in FY2017, ₹3,020.55 lakhs, ₹3,227.89 lakhs and ₹3,082.27 lakhs earlier — the filing notes the rise from ₹3,082.27 lakhs in FY2014. Long-term borrowings were only ₹133.09 lakhs (₹1.33 crore) in FY2018. Almost all of the borrowing sits in the short-term bucket.

On cash: the filing states plainly that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and that sustained negative cash flow could hurt the business and its results. The excerpt does not carry the amounts.

Two further disclosures that sit with the debt: ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans outstanding as at March 31, 2018 that are repayable on demand, and a stated risk that failing to recover trade receivables on time would affect the financial condition.

financials.purpose: Take the restated statements apart: what revenue has done, what profit has done, what the balance sheet carries, and where the two trends disagree.

beats.beat: Control sits with one person. Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue issued, subscribed and paid-up equity share capital.
The rest of the board's stake is nominal: three whole-time directors hold 300 shares each. Hatim Sakerwala, a key management person, holds 9% of the equity as on the date of the draft.

Who runs the finance and compliance functions: Anchal Pachori, 28, a chartered accountant, is chief financial officer and heads accounts and finance; Mohit Soni, 26, an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, is company secretary and compliance officer.

Related-party flows the filing discloses for FY2018: ₹68.4 lakhs of loans taken from key management persons and board members; ₹57.7 lakhs of director remuneration; and ₹324.3 lakhs of outstanding payables to related parties as at 31 March 2018. The filing states it has entered into related-party transactions in the past and may continue to.

Two promoter-linked companies, Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited, were struck off by the Registrar of Companies on March 12, 2016 and March 11, 2016 respectively for non-operation of business.

Two more red-flag disclosures stated in the filing: the company issued equity shares in the previous 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price, and it has appointed no monitoring agency, leaving deployment of funds to management discretion subject to audit committee oversight.

And the clearances: no director is on the RBI list of wilful defaulters, the promoter confirms he has not been declared a wilful defaulter by the RBI or any government authority, and there are no criminal cases or investigations against any director. The filing separately states the company, promoter and directors are involved in litigation pending at various stages.

beats.beat: Define the sector before sizing it: infrastructure as the filing uses the term covers power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development.

The structural fact that matters most for a small contractor: construction is a highly fragmented, working-capital-intensive market contributing roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices. Fragmented means many bidders; working-capital-intensive means cash goes out before it comes back.

The demand numbers the filing cites: India needs ₹50 trillion (US$777.73 billion) of infrastructure investment by 2022; infrastructure spending was 9.0% of GDP in the 12th Five-Year Plan; FDI into construction development from April 2000 to December 2017 was US$24.67 billion; the logistics sector is projected to grow at 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020; and the eight core industries grew 4.2% cumulatively in 2017-18.

What the filing says will drive that demand: government programmes including the 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; eased FDI norms across 15 sectors including real estate and construction; and rising industrialisation, urbanisation, disposable income and population growth.
Who it competes with: the filing says the field includes both organised and unorganised players, and names no competitor.

The headwinds the company lists against itself in its own SWOT: the slow pace of government projects, a working-capital crunch that may affect profitability, and changes in government policy. For a contractor whose client is the government, the first and third are not hypothetical.

industry.heading: The market it sells into
industry.purpose: Give the reader the shape of Indian infrastructure and construction — how big, how fast, who pays, and what the filing itself admits are the headwinds.

beats.beat: Plain orientation: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-focused infrastructure contractor that builds railway platforms and station buildings, bridges and roads, and also runs a ready-mix concrete plant at Kashimira in Thane district, Maharashtra.
The company describes itself as operating in exactly two segments — creation of infrastructure, and operating a ready-mix concrete plant. Everything else in the filing sits inside one of those two.
What is being sold: 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at an issue price the filing leaves blank. The blank matters — with no price, the rupee size of the offer is not disclosed.
Where the money goes: ₹1,130 lakhs (₹11.30 crore) to working capital requirements, plus general corporate purposes for an amount the filing does not state.
Three facts that frame the rest of the piece: the promoter held 90.949% of the pre-issue equity; Indian Railways was 57% of FY2018 revenue; and revenue fell across the restated periods.

intro.purpose: Orient a reader who has never heard of this company: what it builds, where it builds it, what it is selling, and the two or three facts that make the filing worth a look.

beats.beat: The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at an issue price the filing shows as a blank. Until that price is set, the rupee size of the issue and the post-issue capital structure cannot be read off the DRHP.
The objects of the issue, named: meeting working capital requirements, budgeted at ₹1,130 lakhs (₹11.30 crore); and general corporate purposes, for an amount the filing does not disclose.

Why a working-capital object is worth understanding here rather than skimming: the money is not going to a new plant or an acquisition, it is going into the day-to-day gap between paying for a project and being paid for it — the same gap the filing lists as a risk.

A gap to state plainly rather than fill: the excerpt shows 44,28,000 shares on offer and shows proceeds flowing to the company, but it does not name an offer-for-sale selling shareholder or split the shares between fresh issue and offer for sale. Readers should treat the fresh-versus-OFS composition as not established by these excerpts.
Who runs the process: Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited is the lead manager; Bigshare Services Private Limited is the registrar.

Two governance-adjacent disclosures that belong next to the objects: no independent agency was appointed to appraise the proposed project, and no monitoring agency was appointed — deployment of the funds sits with the management and board, monitored by the audit committee.

beats.beat: One customer carries the revenue. Indian Railways was the largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in FY2018, and Western Railway alone was 52% of orders on hand. The filing's own words are that losing Indian Railways as the largest customer would cause a significant dip in revenue.

Winning work is not in the company's hands. Revenue depends on the bids it submits to government and government departments being accepted, and the award goes to the lowest quote. Unsuccessful bids are not a slowdown; they are a direct hit to the financial condition.

The company has been burning cash. The filing states that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and that sustained negative cash flow could adversely affect the business and results.

Short-term obligations and unpaid bills can bite at any time. ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans were outstanding as at March 31, 2018 and are repayable on demand, while short-term borrowings stood at ₹3,537.35 lakhs in FY2018. The filing also flags that failing to recover trade receivables on time would affect the financial condition.

The work is concentrated in one city. The filing warns that a major portion of revenue comes from operations in specific geographic regions, especially Mumbai, and that adverse developments in those regions could hurt revenue and results.

risks.heading: The five risks the filing makes hard to miss
risks.purpose: Pick the risks that are specific to this company, and explain each in one move. Stop at five.

beats.beat: Start with the constraint, because it governs the whole section: the issue price is a blank. The face value is ₹10, and the filing says the issue price is [●] times the face value. There is no number to work backwards from.

The filing does contain a section headed 'Comparison of Accounting Ratios with Peer Group Companies'. The figures captured from pages 54 and 55 sit against financial years — FY2015-16 shows 1.31 and 1.31; FY2016-17 shows 0.63 and 0.63; FY2017-18 shows 12.59 and 3.82; and separate year lines show 4.14, 1.97 and 28.14, with 44.71 and 12.39 also appearing. The excerpts do not carry the column headings that say which of these is EPS, which is NAV per share and which is return on net worth.

Say what that means for the reader rather than guessing: without the column labels and without the names of the peer companies, a like-for-like peer table cannot be built from these excerpts, and the implied price range that would normally follow from it cannot be computed here. The filing's own position is only that the issue price, determined with the lead manager, is justified based on those accounting ratios.

What can be said from the figures that do carry labels: FY2018 revenue of ₹6,053.05 lakhs, profit after adjustments of ₹314.66 lakhs, EBITDA of ₹928.80 lakhs, short-term borrowings of ₹3,537.35 lakhs and a ₹10 face value. Those are the inputs a reader has; the multiple is not in the excerpts.
